For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′}=f(x,y,z)\, & z(a)=d,\end{aligned}
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3{y}^{″} & ={x}^{2}-2{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{′}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=0.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(1)=2, \\ {z}^{′}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3},\, & z(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=3.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=3$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{3-1}{2}=1.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=2$ and $z(1)=0.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ |  |  | $0$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=0 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}=\frac{{1}^{2}-2\cdot 0}{3}=\frac{1}{3} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=0\cdot 1=0 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{3} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+0=2 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=0+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $2$ |  |  | $\frac{1}{3}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=\frac{1}{3} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-2z}{3}=\frac{({2}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{3})}{3}=\frac{10}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{1}{3}\cdot 1=\frac{1}{3} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{10}{9}\cdot 1=\frac{10}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=2+1=3 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=2+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{7}{3} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{10}{9}=\frac{13}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $2$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{10}{9}$ | $\frac{10}{9}$ |
| $3$ | $\frac{7}{3}$ |  |  | $\frac{13}{9}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(3)≈\frac{7}{3}$
and
${y}^{′}(3)=z(3)≈\frac{13}{9}.$
